entries.title: ‘Ask For What You Want’ Is a Key Skill For the 21st Century
entries.summary: "Seeing a new icon in your dock drives home the understanding: this environment is malleable. It can, at last, be anything I want."
entries.content:
On his blog, author Robin Sloan shares observations on working with AI agents to build a native desktop app. He’s cautious and critical of AI, and explains his process to creative people who are wary of it. But, ultimately, he encourages experimentation.

Okay, so. With the help of the AI agent, you make your first app. It bounces merrily in the dock. I want to underscore, what’s important is not that it’s a notes app, or a sleek jukebox, or whatever. You can already get every kind of app. What’s important is that it’s yours. It’s weird and specific, and it won’t change unless you want it to change.

More essays about AI

Benchma(r)king

“James Bridle experiments with combining their practical carpentry skills and the abundant theoretical knowledge of AI to build a chair.”

How AI Replaced Me

“An edtech worker’s account of what got left behind.”

Beyond the Machine

“I want to frame the technology more like an instrument, and get away from GenAI as an intelligence, an ideology, a tool, a crutch, or a weapon.”

entries.title: The Old and The Furious
entries.summary: "As Americans live longer than ever, car crashes involving elderly adults are on the rise. The question is what to do about it—and how many more deadly accidents it will take for us to act."
entries.content:
Americans are living longer these days, long enough to become vehicular terrors behind the wheel in their eighties and nineties, and they’re injuring themselves and others at unprecedented rates. David Howard, with additional reporting from Lloyd Alter, does the math and suggests that simply taking a senior’s licence away is not the answer; America is car-centric and many seniors need to drive in order to grocery shop, attend health appointments, and to meet their social needs. Could autonomous vehicles provide the balance we need between safety and independence?

Already visible on the technological horizon, of course, are self-driving cars, which carry the potential to obviate many of the limitations older drivers face. Mark Needham (not his real name) lives on the fringes of Charlottesville, Virgina. He is 82 and still active: He practices yoga at a local health club, engages in a glassblowing hobby, and dabbles with technology. He and his wife, 80, have lived in the same subdivision for 40 years, and while she’s wrestling with several health issues and is ready to move into a retirement facility, he’s adamantly opposed to it. “My wife is more inclined to being taken care of,” Needham says.

“I’m more inclined to be doing stuff.”

Part of what allows him to maintain his independence: a Tesla that over his two-plus years of ownership has morphed, via a steady stream of software updates, into a largely autonomous vehicle. (Many reviewers and experts still cite the need for improvement with tasks like changing speeds and parking before use becomes widespread.) “It drives better than I drove 30 or 40 years ago,” he says.

More picks on aging

No iPad Till After Dinner, Mom

“Seniors are spending more time than ever on their slop-filled feeds. It’s their adult children’s job to save them.”

The Seniors Against Senior Housing

“America’s elders need more places to live, but even in liberal enclaves that recognize the problem, developers are facing the fiercest foes of all: America’s elders.”

My Father Wants to Age in Place. AI Will Be Watching

“Devices that monitor seniors for safety are appealing to worried loved ones and underresourced home care agencies.”

entries.title: Juiced to the Gills
entries.content:
You have, by now, read something about the Enhanced Games, the steroid-fueled athletic spectacle held this year in Las Vegas. (Perhaps we even recommended it.) But there’s nothing quite like seeing the event through Kent Russell’s eyes as he sneaks high-proof whiskey from his ThermoFlask, considers the physical demands of parenting and his own life’s onrushing decline, and concedes that a drug-enhanced life sounds “pretty fucking dope.”

As of this moment, the sprinters are clean, the Erth bleachers are searing the backs of my thighs, and Michael Bryan is overawing me through the act of locomotion. I sip from my thermos and bask in wonderment that a human body can be made to move that way. Beauty of this kind, which eighteenth-century types correctly filed under the category of the sublime, requires that it exceed me. A thing I could do myself is admirable; a thing that no effort of mine could ever accomplish, that lives permanently past my ceiling, is awesome in the old, strong sense of the word, in which awe is part fear, part love, part recognition that I am small and soft. The unfairness is the source of the wonder. To resent that Bryan is gifted beyond me is to resent that the thing I’m watching is beautiful, which is insane and would require that I demand the world contain nothing larger than myself.

A few recent features about drugs

Toadstools and Toxins

“When I found the mushroom Amanita muscaria being sold in candy wrappers, I uncovered legal loopholes, dangerous dosages and more.”

He Was One of the World’s Most Wanted Men. So He Bought a West African Country.

“How Jos Leijdekkers turned Sierra Leone into a drug-dealer’s paradise.”

The Great Ozempic Experiment

“It’s a new era of D.I.Y. medicine. Now the health establishment needs to catch up.”

entries.title: Raumforderung
entries.summary: "Raumforderung means something big and wrong is making it hard to live."
entries.content:
In this blunt, beautiful, and harrowing essay from Off Assignment, Blossom Gordana Champlain recounts learning of a mass, a foreign body next to her lung after visiting a German hospital. In considering the literal trouble she carries next to her heart, she examines what it means to be foreign, recounting her grandfather, who was trafficked from Ukraine to Germany, and her father, considered a displaced person in 1945 as Europe emerged from the Second World War.

Raumforderung is a medical term arriving in my mind carrying more affect than information. I know that something improper and unwilling is happening. Instead of the valiant ingestion and revolutionary expulsion of the awful outside, instead of room for the paradox by which we all survive, there is crowding and concession. Displaced genes commanded wrongful growth, demanded space which could not be defended, and so was conceded, to a slow invisible thing, the bad truth I could ever only have failed to escape.

More personal essays

Mal à la Tête

“My neurologist says anything can be a headache. Or rather, a headache can cause anything, since all sensations start in the brain.”

Field Notes from a Body

“As I watched I had felt a nameless churn in my gut, some tremor of feeling I couldn’t describe.”

The Essay as Realm

The space of the essay does have edges, but the edges are a little bit ragged and open.

entries.title: We the Vloggers
entries.summary: “First Amendment auditors say they’re fighting for your constitutional rights. But if one shows up at your office—and one very well might—you’re going to want to be prepared.”
entries.content:
Our elected officials should be accountable to the public. Law enforcement officers should be accountable to the public. These are undeniably true. But most of us don’t use that sentiment to defend walking into local government offices with a camera and trying to film employees’ computer screens, or bothering people outside a post office. Welcome to the world of “First Amendment auditors,” a community of . . . well, let’s call them “enthusiastic enforcers of their own conception of what’s allowable on public property.” Get ready for your closeup!

The auditors’ devotion to the U.S. Constitution and suspicion of authority might read to observers as libertarian-coded, but the YouTubers I spoke with claim not to have any partisan motivations. Rather, they’re asserting their right to record as a contrived stress test of whether public officials respect that right. Auditors’ MOs run the gamut. Some clearly seem to be goading police officers, government workers, and passersby into engaging with them. Others take a more stoic tack, refusing to answer questions or saying as little as possible. Still others identify as citizen journalists. Sometimes the audits are a laid-back affair, but the ones that rack up the most views are those where people captured in the video lose it, making themselves unwitting stars of a pseudo–soap opera.

More picks from Slate

The Old and The Furious

“As Americans live longer than ever, car crashes involving elderly adults are on the rise. The question is what to do about it—and how many more deadly accidents it will take for us to act.”

Inside America’s Shoplifting Lab

“In the war on ‘shrink,’ big retailers are turning to one Florida outfit to study shoppers and prevent them from stealing. I went there—and saw far too much.”

The Forgotten Bombing of LaGuardia Airport

“It’s been called ‘one of the greatest cold cases of the 20th century.’ It remains unsolved. But what happened next is almost a worse crime.”

The Florida Alligator Dragnet

“When an alligator kills someone in America, it can make international headlines. What happens to the thousands of gators that people deem ‘nuisances’ does not.”

How the Crossword Conquered America

“Even in a boom time for games, the decidedly old-fashioned puzzles are more popular than ever. I went to the best place on Earth to understand why.”

The Capybaras Aren’t All Right

“The internet’s favorite animal is facing a dark fate.”

entries.title: In the Wilds of the Yukon, a Novelist Faces Herself
entries.summary: "Trekking through the territory on her birthday, Maggie Shipstead reconsiders her relationship to aging and risk."
entries.content:
Maggie Shipstead, whose novel Great Circle was shortlisted for the Booker Prize, decided to celebrate her 43rd birthday with a five-day hiking trip through the backcountry of Canada’s Yukon territory, accompanied by photographer Vicky Sambunaris and a few guides. Away from the cacophony of civilization, among the Dall sheep, the grizzly and her cubs, the caribou, and the moose, Shipstead confronts the so-called limitations of aging, discovering anew that what often prevents us women from seeking arduous adventure is ourselves.

My body felt good, better than I’d expected, better than I’d felt at home, where I spend too much time sitting at a desk. My body likes to move, apparently, to climb and descend; it’s fine with sleeping on the ground. My tricky left knee hurt a little bit, but it has since I was a teenager. I was tired at the end of each day, but hiking all day is tiring. I started to wonder why I had been so quick to decide I was, in the parlance of my parents’ generation, over the hill. Why had I insisted on mourning something I hadn’t actually lost?

More picks about adventure

He Went Out on an Epic Wilderness Adventure. Only His Dogs Came Back.

“He planned a multiyear trek through rivers, forests and snow in the Canadian wilderness. Only his sled dogs returned.”

My I.R.L. Adventures in the Land of the Eagle Cam

“I traveled to Big Bear Lake, home of a viral live feed of an eagle’s nest, and found very human shenanigans.”

What I Found When I Tried to Walk Across Dallas in a Day

“Determined to find adventure in my own backyard, I tramped across my famously pedestrian-averse hometown. The most memorable part turned out to be the serendipitous encounters with neighbors I met along the way.”

entries.title: The Parents Who Never Stop Tracking Their Kids
entries.summary: "Tech has made it easy for parents to surveil their kids all the way through college—and beyond."
entries.content:
What does helicopter parenting look like today? For The Atlantic, Sarah Zhang reports on parents who use location-tracking apps such as Life360 to follow their kids when they’re out in the world—to school, to their friend’s house—if they’re even allowed to venture out at all. Drawing on conversations with parents and experts, Zhang examines what constant surveillance does to both kids and parents, and how safety and anxiety play out in a world that feels very different from the one many of us grew up in. (I’ll note that “kids” here includes people in their 20s: If Zhang’s interviews are any indication, a shocking number of parents track their college- and graduate-age kids.)

When Maureen Paschal, a college counselor in North Carolina, sent her daughter off to college a few years ago, she was promptly invited to join a group chat for moms of the girls living on the same floor. The moms, she recalls, tracked their daughters’ location during sorority rush, watching as they moved from house to house. But the incident that stuck in her mind came one fall morning, when a mom messaged the group chat that her daughter was still in her dorm room. She had a math test in 10 minutes. Could someone ask their kid to go knock on her door?

“I just was like, This is too much. It’s just too much,” Paschal told me. But not everyone thought so. Another mom soon replied: My daughter is on her way.

More stories by Sarah Zhang

When Anesthesia Goes Wrong

“A teenage boy went into surgery for a broken arm and emerged with brain damage. His mother was determined to figure out what had happened.”

DNA Tests Are Uncovering the True Prevalence of Incest

“People are discovering the truth about their biological parents with DNA—and learning that incest is far more common than many think.”

After the Miracle Drug

“Cystic fibrosis once guaranteed an early death—but a medical breakthrough has given many patients a chance to live decades longer than expected. What do they do now?”

entries.title: Give a Fig: A Reading List on Sweet, Wild, Mad Fruits
entries.summary: A lavish spread gathered from a colorful cornucopia. Enjoy!
entries.content:
Thoughtful stories for thoughtless times.

Longreads has published hundreds of original stories—personal essays, reported features, reading lists, and more—and more than 14,000 editor’s picks. And they’re all funded by readers like you. Become a member today.

I once took a workshop conducted by award-winning advertising copywriters. I was the only industry outsider there, just a kid from tech, attending out of interest on my own time and money. When my team submitted our overwrought assignment—an ad for a fictitious mango candy—the instructor took one look and said: Look for the juice.

Salman Rushdie was once asked whether he had any advice for postcolonial writers. “There must be no tropical fruits in the title. No mangoes, no guavas. None of those,” said Rushdie. “Tropical animals are also problematic. Peacock, etc. Avoid that shit.” 

Where I’m from (also where the word mango comes from—மாங்காய், māṅgāi, in Tamil, മാങ്ങ, māṅṅa, in Malayalam, the latter with its rounded, velar-nasal-double consonant deemed unpronounceable by outsiders), you’ve got to deal with that shit sooner or later, and I don’t mean by way of literary theory. Literature may be giving the mango the side-eye, but life is not. Mangoes are good. 

Myth and history, metaphor and mystery, science and commerce, story and language and art, memory, desire, and life itself: There are so many places writing on fruits could go, each one an orchard, that this reading list could sprawl into a book. So I’ve simply gathered a lavish spread from a colorful cornucopia, letting the pieces themselves do the rest.

The Latin verb frui means “to enjoy.” As Black Phillip asks Thomasin in the 2015 film The VVitch: A New-England Folktale, “Wouldst thou like to live deliciously?”

Fruit of the Fall (Philip Getz, Jewish Review of Books, Fall 2023)

Why is painting obsessed with food, and fruits in particular? Explore “A Brief History of Food in European Art” via Google Arts and Culture. And while you’re at it, meet the Italian “fruit detective” who examines Renaissance paintings to find out what fruits have since gone missing from the world, and why.

To me, no apple can beat a mango. But all right, I concede that the fairytale fruit has something going for it, too. Not to mention the dark glamor of being the forbidden fruit from the Tree of Knowledge in the Garden of Eden. Was it, though? Or was that a grape, for its “intoxicating powers,” or a fig, perhaps, because fig leaves, or any one of a hundred other candidates? How did the apple gain such delectable infamy? 

Built around the review of a book he calls a “philological detective story,” Getz’s essay examines the religious and aesthetic history of the forbidden fruit. 

Back in 1997, a horticulturist at Washington State University named Bruce Barritt placed pollen from a Honeycrisp on the stigma of an Enterprise apple flower. Twenty-two years of testing later the Cosmic Crisp apple was released, to great acclaim. The New York Times described it as “dramatically dark, richly flavored and explosively crisp and juicy,” almost sinfully good, one might say.

This wasn’t the first time apples burst cosmically onto the cultural scene. In twelfth-century France, apples began showing up in Christian depictions of “the Fall of Man,” everywhere from the Cathedral of Notre Dame to illuminated Bibles and psalm books. These red and gold apples supplanted the previous identification of grapes and figs as the forbidden fruit with which the serpent tempted Eve and Eve tempted Adam. Grapes and figs are low-hanging fruit, biblically speaking. The Land of Israel, for instance, is described as “a land of wheat and barley, of vines, figs, and pomegranates, a land of olive trees and honey” (Deut. 8:8)—but not of apples, not here or anywhere else in the Bible. Where did they come from?

A Secret, Symbolic History of Pomegranates (Kate Lebo, Literary Hub, April 2021)

“At no time did I stop eating maraschino cherries. This was, in a way, like smoking would be later: an abstract poison whose intake, because it had not yet killed me, made me immortal.” Another extract from the Lebo book for Harper’s Magazine: “Pit of Despair.”

My introduction to a mad fruit called medlar, and to Lebo’s The Book of Difficult Fruit (see M for Medlar), was as follows: “A shriveled, rose-hip-like bulb about the size of a fig, called in Shakespeare’s time ‘open-arse’ because its calyx looks (sort of) like the pucker of an anus. Called open-arse or cul de chien today because once one gets a nickname like ‘open-arse’ or ‘dog’s ass,’ even centuries can’t erase it. That medlars are not ripe until they rot—a process called bletting—contributes to their assness, I guess.” 

The book’s subtitle is a clue: “Arguments for the Tart, Tender, and Unruly.” This fertile essay is from P for Pomegranate (a fruit whose internal structure gives the poor, butthurt medlar a run for its money).

When Persephone returns to her mother, the underworld is still on her. . . . Persephone has seen the dead, married their king, eaten three or four or seven seeds of his pomegranate. Her mother, the harvest goddess Demeter—having been flattened by grief, having refused to let new crops grow until her daughter returns, having starved mortals until the gods fear no one will survive to leave offerings, having, in another version of the myth, convinced Zeus to make Hades give Persephone back—welcomes home a changed girl, wizened and spooky, uneasy in her mother’s empire of green. A married girl who hears and speaks of a world Demeter can’t understand. “The voice is paler than the lips it leaves,” says Demeter in Edith Wharton’s retelling, her joy fading to confusion.

Pomegranates are unusual fruits, “no more than a closet of juicy seeds,” as Jane Grigson describes them. Poets have been known to compare those seeds to jewels.

Oranges-I & Oranges-II (John McPhee, The New Yorker, May 1966)

“Take an orange.” Fifty years after McPhee’s journey, Wyatt Williams undertakes one of his own for the Oxford American just to see what’s up with those oranges: “After Oranges.” (The quote in the intro is from a paywalled interview in The Paris Review, seen via this essay.)

“That’s all I said—oranges. I didn’t mention juice, I didn’t mention trees, I didn’t mention the tropics. Just—oranges. Oh yes! Oh yes! [William Shawn] says. That’s very good. The next thing I knew I was in Florida talking to orange growers.”

Here’s the two-part essay that became Pulitzer-winner McPhee’s stone-cold classic Oranges—retro, refreshing Americana with an exacting, adoring eye on the world. And once you’ve read the essays (or the book) for the oranges, take another look to see how he’s done it—a masterclass in literary reportage from a pioneer of creative nonfiction.

An orange grown in Florida usually has a thin and tightly fitting skin, and it is also heavy with juice. Californians say that if you want to eat a Florida orange you have to get into a bathtub first. California oranges are light in weight and have thick skins that break easily and come off in hunks. The flesh inside is marvellously sweet, and the segments almost separate themselves. In Florida, it is said that you can run over a California orange with a ten-ton truck and not even wet the pavement. The differences from which these hyperboles arise will prevail in the two states even if the type of orange is the same. In arid climates, like California’s, oranges develop a thick albedo, which is the white part of the skin. Florida is one of the two or three most rained-upon states in the United States. California uses the Colorado River and similarly impressive sources to irrigate its oranges, but of course irrigation can only do so much. The annual difference in rainfall between the Florida and California orange-growing areas is one million one hundred and forty thousand gallons per acre. For years, California was the leading orange state, but Florida surpassed California in 1942, and grows three times as many oranges now. California oranges, for their part, can safely be called three times as beautiful.

Watch Out for the Top Banana (Larry Tye, Cabinet, Fall 2006)

In 1928, federal troops in Ciénaga, Colombia, shot and killed striking banana workers and their families. The United Fruit Company, exerting significant political and economic pressure, had portrayed the strike as a subversive threat. Gabriel García Márquez, a journalist there at the time, later included a nightmarish depiction of the Banana Massacre in One Hundred Years of Solitude. “‘Look at the mess we’ve got ourselves into,’ Colonel Aureliano Buendía said at that time, ‘just because we invited a gringo to eat some bananas.’” 

We’ve heard the term “banana republic,” disparagingly used to refer to countries exploited by foreign entities (corporations, militaries, governments) for economic profit and political power. The real stories behind the original banana republics and the human suffering involved are less well known. Tye, a Boston Globe journalist, tracks down primary sources from the Library of Congress to build a compelling portrait of how Edward Bernays (a nephew of Sigmund Freud) and the United Fruit Company used psychology and the media to take control of entire nations in Central and South America, such as Honduras, Costa Rica, Guatemala, and Colombia. Yes, banana propaganda. Recipes were involved, as was the CIA. Are you looking at the sweet, yellow, imported fruit in your kitchen bowl right now?

This essay is drawn from Cabinet’s special issue on Fruits. Check out its other interesting, idiosyncratic offerings.

The United Fruit Company was born over a bottle of rum. In 1870, Lorenzo Dow Baker, skipper of the Boston schooner Telegraph, pulled into Jamaica for a taste of the island’s famous distilled alcohol and a load of bamboo. While he was drinking, a local tradesman came by offering green bananas; Baker bought 160 bunches at twenty-five cents each. He resold them in New York for up to $3.25 a bunch, a deal so sweet he couldn’t resist doing it again. By 1885, eleven ships were flying under the banner of the new Boston Fruit Company, bringing to the United States ten million bunches of bananas a year. United Fruit was formed in 1899, with assets that included more than 210,000 acres of land across the Caribbean and Central America and enough political clout that Honduras, Costa Rica, and other countries in the region became known as “banana republics.”

The Incredible Fig (Meg Lowman, Nautilus, July 2021)

In Singapore, the durian is considered a delicacy. That hasn’t stopped the government from banning it outright on public transportation and in hotels. Its notoriety is down to its sulfurous scent of unmatched pungency. Here, durian-loving scientists investigate.

If you like figs, you’re in august company. Cleopatra is said to have loved them. When she planned to take her own life, she chose to hide the deadly asp in a basket of figs. But this essay might make you see them in a different light. 

The fig isn’t really a fruit at all, but a syconium (a vessel containing tiny flowers) in interspecies communion with a female wasp. Lowman, a biologist and pioneering canopy ecologist, explores the history and biology of the fig (which she loves), sacrificing none of its complex science, sexiness, or strangeness. The mother wasp lies in her floral tomb, and new life chews its way out.

Mature Ficus (including banyans) produce thousands of fruits, an important food source in tropical food webs. Fertile figs, like the ones we eat, are distinct because of their unique fleshy, hollow receptacle with an inner surface laced with tiny flowers or fruitlets. All species have tiny male and female flowers that develop on the inside wall of a syconium, which eventually becomes a fruit. A tiny female wasp of the Agaonidae family enters a hole in the top of the syconium and passes through a tunnel lined with downward-facing scales that only allow one-way travel. The wasp finds two types of female flowers inside: stalked, short-styled flowers and long-styled flowers that are not stalked. While she pollinates the flowers, the wasp also lays her eggs and then dies. After a few weeks, her offspring hatch, and wingless males mate with winged females, then chew an exit tunnel that allows the females to fly to another fig and repeat the process. The females pick up pollen from recently matured male flowers as they exit. Some botanists originally thought all 800 species required a specific pollinator wasp, but more recent molecular analyses reveal that 119 fig species shared multiple pollinator wasp species. When a wasp dies inside the fig after pollination, enzymes (called ficain) break down the carcass; consequently, anyone who eats figs is also consuming wasp biomass.

Dark Fruit: A Cultural and Personal History of the Plum (Anca L. Szilágyi, Los Angeles Review of Books, October 2016)

If you look closely at the central panel of the Hieronymous Bosch triptych called The Garden of Earthly Delights, you’ll see a great number of humans in various states of mutual ravishment with fruits, especially strawberries. Walter S. Gibson has a whole paper on what’s going on. 

“The plums, to me, are like a lesser-told story that is no less magical—perhaps more so in its rediscovery, because of its rediscovery. Not pomegranates, not apples, but plums as temptation.”

This intimate understanding of plums is the key to Szilágyi’s essay. Memories and stories, both individual and collective, gather under delicately rendered micro-chapters, traversing her Romanian childhood and her grandmother’s cooking, politics, literature, art, agriculture, Chinese poetry, and her life in the United States: “Eat, Memory; Rituals; Favors; Hunger; Wild Plums; Sex and Death; Fairy Tale-Red Fruit; The World Seems More Real.”

Five years after the fall of communism, my family visited Romania, the old country, for the first time since my parents left in the 1970s. We drove counterclockwise around the place, in a two-car caravan, starting and ending in Bucharest. On one of our last days, my father’s mother insisted we drive through the Carpathians in the pitch-black night, as she was eager to meet a friend the next day. I gripped the edge of my seat, watched the high beams of our cars skim the edges of steep cliffs, and then buried my head in my mother’s lap, hoping it would all be over soon. The next morning, safely away from the hairpin turns of the mountains and among rolling hills—farmland, orchard country—my grandmother asked my father to stop the car. There were no landmarks to indicate a meeting place. But as we stretched our legs, my grandmother waved at a figure in the distance, and a man’s flat cap emerged first from behind a hill. His tan arms clutched something to his chest and he rushed toward her with a sloshing Pepsi bottle full of clear liquid: tsuica. Homemade plum brandy. Moonshine. Into her suitcase it went, carefully transported back to the States so that it might properly “disinfect” us before each dinner.

The Serviceberry (Robin Wall Kimmerer, Emergence, October 2022)

In the news: “We never used to think twice about seeing orange and peach trees, green fields, grapes and figs. These things were simply part of our lives. Now when we see them, we are surprised,” says Saleh Kilani, a 70-year-old olive farmer in Gaza. According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), there’s another casualty of Israel’s war: “89% of orchard and other trees (including 90% of olive trees).”

Kimmerer and the birds—Cedar Waxwings, Catbirds, Bluebirds, her namesake Robins (she capitalizes the names of flora and fauna)—have all gathered for the spring-summer harvest of the Serviceberry. The etymology of its name, its beauty and delight, and the sheer abundance of nature encourage Kimmerer, a Potawatomi botanist, stuffing her mouth and “chortling with happiness,” to consider the gift economy and its modes of exchange—gratitude and generous reciprocity.

In Potawatomi, it is called Bozakmin, which is a superlative: the best of the berries. I agree with my ancestors on the rightness of that name. Imagine a fruit that tastes like a Blueberry crossed with the satisfying heft of an Apple, a touch of rosewater and a minuscule crunch of almond-flavored seeds. They taste like nothing a grocery store has to offer: wild, complex with a chemistry that your body recognizes as the real food it’s been waiting for.

For me, the most important part of the word Bozakmin is “min,” the root for “berry.” It appears in our Potawatomi words for Blueberry, Strawberry, Raspberry, even Apple, Maize, and Wild Rice. The revelation in that word is a treasure for me, because it is also the root word for “gift.” In naming the plants who shower us with goodness, we recognize that these are gifts from our plant relatives, manifestations of their generosity, care, and creativity. When we speak of these not as things or products or commodities, but as gifts, the whole relationship changes. I can’t help but gaze at them, cupped like jewels in my hand, and breathe out my gratitude.

GOOSEBERRIES

“You sit on the veranda having tea, and your ducks swim in the pond, and everything smells delicious and—the gooseberries are ripening.”

Anton Chekhov originally published the short story “Gooseberries” in the Russkaya Mysl magazine in August 1898. George Saunders includes the full Avrahm Yarmolinsky translation and lovingly illuminates it in A Swim in the Pond in the Rain: In Which Four Russians Give a Master Class on Writing, Reading, and Life. 

Vladimir Nabokov once said of Chekhov: “Things for him were funny and sad at the same time, but you would not see their sadness if you did not see their fun, because both were linked up.”

Kanya Kanchana is a writer from India.

Editor: Krista Stevens

Copyeditor: Brendan Fitzgerald
